To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inducible intracardiac and intrapulmonary shunts exist and can be modulated by a number of physiological and pathophysiological factors, and that these shunts are associated with arterial hypoxemia.
inducible intrathoracic shunts in the form of large diameter intraparenchymal arteriovenous connections exist in healthy humans, are closed at rest and can open during hyperkinetic conditions.
inducible intrathoracic arteriovenous shunts are a potential pathway for paradoxical embolization in patients without intracardiac or large pulmonary arteriovenus malformations.

the identification, characterization, and modulation of the pulmonary pathways that regulate the transpulmonary passage of emboli in healthy humans.
understanding how pulmonary pathways and mechanisms regulate the shunting of blood from pulmonary to systemic circulation.
understanding how pulmonary arteriovenus anastomoses function and how they can be modulated to prevent or reduce neurologic sequelae in patients following routine surgical procedures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inducible intracardiac and pulmonary arteriovenious communications are present in the majority of healthy humans and are modulated by oxygenation and exercise.
inducible intracardiac and intrapulmonary shunting are not only present in humans, but can be modulated by exercise and by the fraction of inspired air.
in healthy humans, there are inducible large-diameter intrapulmonary vascular shunts that can open during hyperemia, hypoxemia and body positioning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulmonary microcirculation is not a perfect sieve and there are pathways for emboli to reach the systemic circulation in the absence of intrapulmonary shunts.
the pulmonary vasculature has a dynamic and complex anatomy and physiology that is not fully appreciated in clinical practice.
